label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, provider-outage, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 9 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Its diagnosis named no action, so nobody was asked to approve one. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing: this fault's cause is not a deploy.

case.name: provider-outage
case.title: Payments fail: the provider hangs, and our circuit breaker fails fast
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: the provider's charge and refund API hangs (5 s, then 503): our payments API's calls to it time out, each after 3 attempts, until its circuit breaker opens, after 5 calls in a row got no answer; from then on it fails fast, answering 503 'outcome unknown' at once without calling the provider, and lets one trial call through 10 s after it opened, and again after each trial that fails.
case.remedy: nothing to change on our side: the provider must recover (escalate to it). Meanwhile the circuit breaker keeps the API answering at once, and closes again when a trial call gets an answer. After it recovers, the payments and refunds left pending need a decision (retry them with their keys, or mark them failed): a refund left pending blocks new refunds on its payment until it settles

alert.name: PaymentsErrorsHigh
alert.summary: Payments are failing: over the last minute, 97% of the answers to POST /payments on payments-api were 5xx (10.59 per second), above the threshold of 20%. Payments are slow: over the last minute, the p95 latency of POST /payments on payments-api was 3.6 s, above the threshold of 2 s.

diagnosis.hypothesis: The payment provider (fake-provider) is degraded. It hangs on a share of POST /v1/payments calls and returns 500 on others (c4). payments-api waits 3 s per attempt and tries 3 times, so one hung payment request takes about 9.6 s (c7) and pushes p95 above 2 s. The timeouts and 500s tripped the circuit breaker (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on). From about 06:42 every POST /payments and refund fails fast with 503, and payments are left pending (c1, c2). The breaker is doing its job: it sheds load while the provider fails. The cause is upstream, not a change of ours. Timed-out calls apparently carry no status code in the client histogram, which is likely why the provider looked fast there (p95 about 5 ms, c5). Still open: why the provider hangs, which is outside our view, and whether the hung calls created charges on the provider's side.

evidence.shows: POST /payments 503s rose from 0.05/s to 11.5/s at 06:42, while 201s fell. Refunds began returning 503 at the same time.
payments-api errors read 'provider unavailable; payment left pending': the circuit breaker is open and /v1/payments is not sent.

All services, the provider included, were created together at 06:40:26. No single deploy of ours stands out: payments-api runs PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=returned.
The provider returned 500 on about 10% of the calls that got an answer, then traffic to it stopped once the breaker opened.
Answered provider calls are fast (p95 about 5 ms), so the latency is not slow answers. Timeouts appear to be missing from this histogram.
POST /payments traces took 3 s, 6 s and 9.6 s, which are multiples of one 3 s timeout.
One payment made 3 attempts to fake-provider /v1/payments. Each ended in a ReadTimeout after about 3 s, about 9.6 s in total, and the request returned 503.

proposed_fix.summary: No rollback: none of our deploys or settings caused this, and the breaker is protecting us. Escalate to the provider about its timeouts and 500s. Keep the breaker on. Once the provider recovers and the breaker closes, reconcile the payments left pending (for example pmt_000245 and pmt_0004xx). Run money_check to find charges that the hung calls may have created on the provider's side. Consider recording timeouts in the client-latency metric, and a shorter timeout or fewer retries, so one request cannot take 9.6 s.

diagnosis.blast_radius: Doing nothing leaves payments and refunds failing with 503 until the provider recovers, and leaves pending payments to reconcile. Turning the breaker off would only bring back slow, failing requests and add load on the provider.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: No change is made. If later tuning of timeouts or retries makes things worse, restore the previous payments-api settings from the deploy log.
